summary:
The Bahamas decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct on 16 May 1991 through the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act. Nothing in the sources indicates that a visitor can be prosecuted for consensual sexual conduct, and no pattern of police targeting of visitors is documented.

Transgender and intersex residents and visitors hold no statutory protection. Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United stated this absence plainly when it launched the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign on 27 April 2016, and member Torri Culmer has advocated against job termination for trans and intersex workers. The gap is statutory: no enacted non-discrimination provision covering gender identity appears anywhere in the sources. The Constitution's prohibition against discrimination does not cover sexual orientation or gender identity, and the 2006 Constitutional Reform Commission did not regard sexual orientation as deserving protection, with efforts to include it in a proposed Constitution blocked by members citing religious opposition.

Statutory protection remains narrow. The Data Protection (Privacy of Personal Information) Act 2003 lists "sexual life" as sensitive personal data, and a 2001 Employment Bill clause banning sexual-orientation workplace discrimination was removed shortly after passage. Discrimination in healthcare or education on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal, and there are no national hate-crime laws.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal. The Marriage Act defines marriage as between a man and a woman, same-sex households are denied the rights given to opposite-sex married couples, and in 2011 former Minister of State Zhivargo Laing stated a marriage is void if between persons of the same sex, calling this a community standard. Former Prime Minister Perry Christie stated in 2013 he did not believe in same-sex marriage and in 2016 said a referendum would not legalize it, defining marriage as between male and female determined at birth. The 2016 referendum bills were not inclusive of transgender or intersex people.

Official hostility has been expressed publicly. Government member Leslie Miller called for the 'Exile of Transgender out of the Bahamas,' urging financial contributions to relocate transgender people to a private island and pledging $1,000 toward it.

One official statement points the other way. In May 1998 National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson announced that the military, prison service and police do not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation, and LGBT citizens face no prohibition on serving in those forces.

The criminal code sets age of consent at 16 for heterosexual acts and 18 for same-sex acts.

Violent targeting of a gay visitor has been documented. On 8 May 2017 Adrian Brown, 24, Jamaica-born and US-resident, was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being targeted and beaten because he is gay at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival, and he wants charges laid. A 2009 murder victim, a homosexual HIV-positive man, was killed by a defendant acquitted using a "gay panic" defence, and nine murders of gay men between 2001 and 2015 remain unsolved.

Public space for LGBT socialising is constrained. No exclusively gay bars or clubs exist; the Nassau scene is underground, and LGBT groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden. Police raided a gay party in downtown Nassau on 6 October 2007 with no arrests, and the Ministry of Tourism later apologized. Groups of LGBT tourists have been protested, including church group opposition to a 2004 cruise and a 1998 protest against a lesbian cruise; in September 2007 the Bahamas Christian Council formed an anti-gay committee over a request to a local cable company to carry the LGBTQ channel Logo. The Plays and Films Control Board banned Brokeback Mountain in March 2006 and attempted to block a public-square screening of Children of God on 24 June 2011, though the government overruled it.

The Communications Act 2009 empowers URCA to issue codes of practice against content likely to incite hatred or vilify persons on the basis of sexual preference.

Social attitudes are markedly disapproving. Surveys record 85.5% strongly disapproving of same-sex marriage in 2015 with 10.6% approving, and over 84% strongly disapproving of a gay or lesbian politician in 2013 with 12% positive. Many Bahamians belong to conservative Christian denominations treating homosexuality and cross-dressing as decadence, and politicians have been leery of publicly supporting LGBT-rights legislation. In 2016 the Canadian government issued travel advice warning gay couples about the risk of homophobia in the Bahamas. In 2005 an 18-year-old beauty queen had her crown stripped after confirming she was a lesbian.

No HIV-specific or trans-specific care provisions are recorded in the sources.
tangentialFactors:
The Bahamas presents a mixed picture compared with regional neighbours: consensual same-sex conduct has been legal since 1991, earlier than many Caribbean jurisdictions, yet no hate-crime statute or gender-identity non-discrimination protection exists.

Violence risk appears tied to visibility at large public events rather than routine policing. The 2017 carnival assault on a gay visitor and the unsolved murders of gay men between 2001 and 2015 indicate a gap between formal decriminalisation and effective protection.

Official statements cut in both directions. The 1998 ministerial assurance of non-discrimination in the security services sits alongside a sitting parliamentarian's 2010s call to exile transgender people and repeated prime-ministerial opposition to same-sex marriage.

Foreign governments have assessed the risk as real enough to warrant travel advice: Canada warned gay couples in 2016 about the risk of homophobia.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2017 assault on Adrian Brown resulted in charges being laid is not recorded in the sources; he is reported as wanting charges laid.

The sources do not state whether the nine unsolved murders of gay men between 2001 and 2015 have since been reopened or reviewed.

No information is available in the inventory on how gender markers on Bahamian passports or other identity documents are amended, or what a foreign visitor whose documents do not match their presentation should expect at port entry.

Whether the 1998 ministerial non-discrimination statement regarding the military, prison service and police remains current government policy is not sourced.

The inventory does not indicate whether any hate-crime or gender-identity legislation has been introduced since the most recent cited sources.
